courseTitle: Physics 2: Fluids, Heat, Electricity, Light and Atoms
title: Isobaric, Isochoric, Isothermal and Adiabatic Processes
short: Each process holds one thing fixed, which decides how Q, W and ΔU split.
trouble: Students think an isothermal process has no heat flow, mixing it up with an adiabatic one.

blocks.html: The first law $\Delta U = Q + W$ holds for every process, but it has three unknowns. Real processes are often simple enough to fix one of them: the volume, the pressure, the temperature, or the heat. Each choice decides how the energy splits.

For a monatomic ideal gas, $U = \tfrac{3}{2}nRT = \tfrac{3}{2}PV$. Hold $V$ fixed and no work is done, so all heat becomes internal energy. Hold $T$ fixed and $U$ cannot change, so $Q = -W$: heat must flow in to pay for the work. Allow no heat (insulate the gas, or act too fast for heat to flow) and $\Delta U = W$: work done on the gas heats it, and a gas that does work cools. Hold $P$ fixed and both happen: heat raises $U$ and pays for the work.

blocks.cap: Monatomic ideal gas. Isothermal still has heat flow; adiabatic has none.

blocks.html: Isochoric: $W = 0$. Isobaric: $W = -P\Delta V$. Isothermal: $\Delta U = 0$, so $Q = -W$. Adiabatic: $Q = 0$, so $\Delta U = W$. Then use $\Delta U = Q + W$ for whatever is left.

blocks.name: ph-pv
blocks.cap: Isothermal expansion: heat flows in while the gas does work, so $T$ stays the same.

blocks.name: ph-pv
blocks.cap: Adiabatic expansion from the same start: no heat flows in, so the gas cools and its pressure drops faster.

blocks.html: Both are in the Energy and the First Law chapter of the Science Lab, which writes $\Delta U = Q - W$ with $W$ done by the gas.

blocks.title: Heating in a rigid tank
blocks.q: How much heat warms $0.50\,\text{mol}$ of argon by $40\,\text{K}$ at constant volume?

blocks.title: Expanding at constant pressure
blocks.q: A monatomic ideal gas expands at $100\,\text{kPa}$ from $2.0\,\text{L}$ to $5.0\,\text{L}$. Find $W$, $\Delta U$ and $Q$.

blocks.title: A bicycle pump
blocks.q: Air in a pump is compressed so quickly that no heat escapes, with $200\,\text{J}$ of work done on it. Find $\Delta U$.
steps: The internal energy rises, so the air gets hotter. That is why a pump's barrel warms up.

blocks.html: Mixing up isothermal and adiabatic. Isothermal means the temperature stays fixed, and that takes heat flow: heat in during expansion, out during compression. Adiabatic means no heat flows, so the temperature must change. Check: if $T$ is constant, ask where the heat went; if $Q = 0$, ask why $T$ changed.
